Third: "For the accustomed security of the Quraysh, (the protection of) My Sanctuary and their custody of My House." This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan.

Fourth: "For the accustomed security of what He mentioned concerning the journey of winter and summer in their livelihoods." This was said by Makhul.

One: It is a connecting *lam* (*lam al-sillah*) referring back to the preceding surah, from their words ﴿Have you not considered how﴾ up to His saying ﴿and made them like eaten straw﴾, then ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾. 'Umar and Ubayy ibn Ka'b did not separate the two surahs, and they would recite them as a single surah, considering them one surah, meaning: "Have you not considered, for the accustomed security of the Quraysh…"

[p. 346]

Two: The *lam* is a connecting particle referring to what follows it, His saying ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, and the meaning is: "For the favour upon the Quraysh, let them worship the Lord of this House." This was said by the people of Basra. 'Ikrimah recited *li-yalfa Quraysh* (that the Quraysh may be accustomed), and he used to find fault with whoever recited ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾. Some of the people of Makkah recited *ilaf Quraysh*, and they cited the verse of Abu Talib advising his brother Abu Lahab concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

*So do not abandon him as long as you live, to one who is honoured, and be a man of valour and chastity.*
*He drives away the enemies from a Hashimite band; is there not among the people anyone better than them in accustomed security (*ilaf*)?*

As for "Quraysh" in the sense of the one who bore him (*talidu-hu*), they are the children of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. It is said they are the children of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, and whoever is not born of Fihr is not of the Quraysh. According to the well-known view, the children of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah and those born of them are of the Quraysh, even if they were not of the children of Fihr. They had been scattered outside the Sanctuary, so Qusayy ibn Kilab gathered them in the Sanctuary until they took it as their dwelling. The poet said:

*Our father Qusayy was called "the Gatherer" (*mujammi'*), by whom God gathered the tribes of Fihr.*

They differed concerning the reason they were named "Quraysh," in four opinions:

First: Because they gathered together after being dispersed, and *al-taqrish* means gathering. From it is the saying of the poet:

*Brothers who gathered (*qarrashu*) their sins against us, in a tale of their age and of old.*

Second: Because they were merchants who ate from their earnings, and *al-taqrish* means earning.

Third: That they would search (*yufattishun*) the pilgrims for one in need and would meet his need, and *al-qirsh* means searching. The poet said:

*O scorner who searches (*al-muqarrish*) about us before 'Amr, is there any forbearance in him?*

Fourth: That "Quraysh" is the name of a sea creature, among the strongest of its creatures; they were named Quraysh for its strength, and because it eats and is not eaten, and rises above and is not overcome. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who cited the verse of the poet:

*Thus among the servants is the living Quraysh,*
*who devour the lands with a thorough devouring,*
*and for them at the end of time is a Prophet,*
*the slaying among them is abundant, and the cutting down (of the foe).*
*He fills the earth with horses and men,*
*they drive the riding-beasts in a close gathering,*
*they eat the lean and the fat and do not leave (anything),*
*a day in two wings of feathers.*

*Quraysh is the one who dwells in the sea,*
*by it Quraysh was named "Quraysh".*

*It has dominion by its height in the depths of the sea,*
*over all the seas, armies.*

﴿Their accustomed security for the journey of winter and summer﴾: The Quraysh had, every year, two journeys. The *rihlah* (journey) is the travel, because of the hardship of travelling and halting in it: one journey in summer and one journey in winter, seeking trade and gain.

Regarding the journeys of winter and summer, there are two opinions:

One: Both journeys were to Palestine, but the winter journey was by sea, seeking warmth, and the summer journey was to Busra and Adhri'at, seeking cool air. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

Two: The winter journey was to Yemen, because it is a hot land, and the summer journey was to Syria, because it is a cold land. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

If it is asked, what is the meaning of God reminding them of the journeys of winter and summer? There are two answers:

One: That in their travels they were safe from the Arabs, because they were the People of the Sanctuary. So He reminded them of this so that they would know His favour upon them in their security, while others feared.

Two: Because they earned, and so they were prosperous, fed others, and gave to the needy (*yasiluna*), as the poet said about them:

*O man who changes his saddle (*rahl*), why did you not stop with the family of 'Abd Manaf?*

*Those who take the covenant from its horizons,*
*and those who set out on the journey of accustomed security (*ilaf*).*

*And those who give the ruined (*al-ra'ishun*)—and there is no one who gives the ruined—*
*and those who say "Come hither" to the guests.*

*And those who mix their rich with their poor,*
*until their poor becomes as one who is sufficient.*

*'Amr al-'Ula crumbled the bread for his people,*
*while the men of Makkah were in drought, emaciated.*

Thus God reminded them of this favour.

[p. 348]

*Winter in Makkah, a blessing,*
*and its summer in al-Ta'if.*

This is among the great favours, that a people have a hot region that repels the cold of winter from them, and a cold region that repels the heat of summer from them. So God reminded them of this favour.

﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾: God commanded them to worship Him. Regarding His identifying Himself to them as "the Lord of this House," there are two aspects:

One: Because they had idols, so He distinguished Himself from them.

Two: That they were honoured over all the Arabs by the House, so He reminded them of this as a reminder of His favour.

Regarding the meaning of this command, and the *fa'* (so) in His saying ﴿so let them worship﴾, there are four aspects:

First: "So let them worship the Lord of this House," because He bestowed upon them the journeys of winter and summer.

Second: "So let them become accustomed to the worship of the Lord of this House, as they became accustomed to the journeys of winter and summer."

Third: "So let them worship the Lord of this House, because He fed them from hunger and secured them from fear."

Fourth: "So let them abandon the journeys of winter and summer for the worship of the Lord of this House, for He feeds them from hunger and secures them from fear, so that they may devote themselves, by remaining, to supporting His Messenger and defending His religion."

First: He fed them from hunger by the wealth He gave them and the provisions He brought to them. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Second: He fed them from hunger by granting the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) concerning them, when he said: ﴿and provide them with fruits﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: That a famine afflicted them in the Jahiliyyah, so God put into the hearts of the Abyssinians to bring them food, and they brought it. The Quraysh feared them and thought they had come to fight them, so they went out to them on guard. But they had brought them food and assisted them with provisions. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿who fed them from hunger﴾.

[p. 349]

﴿And secured them from fear﴾: Regarding this there are four opinions:

First: He secured them from the fear of the Arabs that they might plunder or fight them, out of honour for the sanctity of the Sanctuary, in response to the prior supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: From the fear of the Abyssinians with the Elephant. This was said by al-A'mash.

Third: He secured them from the fear of leprosy (*al-judham*). This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Sufyan al-Thawri.

Fourth: It means He secured the Quraysh so that the caliphate would be only among them. This was said by 'Ali, may God be pleased with him.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 106, verses 1–4:**

[p. 345] **Surah Quraysh**

Makkiyyah according to most scholars, and Madaniyyah according to al-Dahhak.

Regarding His saying, ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾, *al-iylaf* (accustomed security) is derived from *alifa, ya'lafu*, meaning a customary habit to which one is accustomed. From the same root is the phrase *i'talafa al-qawm* (the people became united).

Regarding His saying, ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾, there are four opinions:

First: "My favour upon the Quraysh," because God's favour upon them was that He made them accustomed to (or united them in) this. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

Second: "For the accustomed security God granted them, because He made them accustomed to it (*ālafahum*)." This was said by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad.

Third: "For the accustomed security of the Quraysh, (the protection of) My Sanctuary and their custody of My House." This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan.

Fourth: "For the accustomed security of what He mentioned concerning the journey of winter and summer in their livelihoods." This was said by Makhul.

Regarding the *lam* in ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾, there are two opinions:

One: It is a connecting *lam* (*lam al-sillah*) referring back to the preceding surah, from their words ﴿Have you not considered how﴾ up to His saying ﴿and made them like eaten straw﴾, then ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾. So its meaning is that what He did to the People of the Elephant was for the sake of the accustomed security of the Quraysh. This was said by Tha'lab. 'Umar and Ubayy ibn Ka'b did not separate the two surahs, and they would recite them as a single surah, considering them one surah, meaning: "Have you not considered, for the accustomed security of the Quraysh…"

[p. 346]

Two: The *lam* is a connecting particle referring to what follows it, His saying ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, and the meaning is: "For the favour upon the Quraysh, let them worship the Lord of this House." This was said by the people of Basra. 'Ikrimah recited *li-yalfa Quraysh* (that the Quraysh may be accustomed), and he used to find fault with whoever recited ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾. Some of the people of Makkah recited *ilaf Quraysh*, and they cited the verse of Abu Talib advising his brother Abu Lahab concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

*So do not abandon him as long as you live, to one who is honoured, and be a man of valour and chastity.*
*He drives away the enemies from a Hashimite band; is there not among the people anyone better than them in accustomed security (*ilaf*)?*

As for "Quraysh" in the sense of the one who bore him (*talidu-hu*), they are the children of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. It is said they are the children of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, and whoever is not born of Fihr is not of the Quraysh. According to the well-known view, the children of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah and those born of them are of the Quraysh, even if they were not of the children of Fihr. They had been scattered outside the Sanctuary, so Qusayy ibn Kilab gathered them in the Sanctuary until they took it as their dwelling. The poet said:

*Our father Qusayy was called "the Gatherer" (*mujammi'*), by whom God gathered the tribes of Fihr.*

They differed concerning the reason they were named "Quraysh," in four opinions:

First: Because they gathered together after being dispersed, and *al-taqrish* means gathering. From it is the saying of the poet:

*Brothers who gathered (*qarrashu*) their sins against us, in a tale of their age and of old.*

Second: Because they were merchants who ate from their earnings, and *al-taqrish* means earning.

Third: That they would search (*yufattishun*) the pilgrims for one in need and would meet his need, and *al-qirsh* means searching. The poet said:

*O scorner who searches (*al-muqarrish*) about us before 'Amr, is there any forbearance in him?*

Fourth: That "Quraysh" is the name of a sea creature, among the strongest of its creatures; they were named Quraysh for its strength, and because it eats and is not eaten, and rises above and is not overcome. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who cited the verse of the poet:

*Thus among the servants is the living Quraysh,*
*who devour the lands with a thorough devouring,*
*and for them at the end of time is a Prophet,*
*the slaying among them is abundant, and the cutting down (of the foe).*
*He fills the earth with horses and men,*
*they drive the riding-beasts in a close gathering,*
*they eat the lean and the fat and do not leave (anything),*
*a day in two wings of feathers.*

*Quraysh is the one who dwells in the sea,*
*by it Quraysh was named "Quraysh".*

*It has dominion by its height in the depths of the sea,*
*over all the seas, armies.*

﴿Their accustomed security for the journey of winter and summer﴾: The Quraysh had, every year, two journeys. The *rihlah* (journey) is the travel, because of the hardship of travelling and halting in it: one journey in summer and one journey in winter, seeking trade and gain.

Regarding the journeys of winter and summer, there are two opinions:

One: Both journeys were to Palestine, but the winter journey was by sea, seeking warmth, and the summer journey was to Busra and Adhri'at, seeking cool air. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

Two: The winter journey was to Yemen, because it is a hot land, and the summer journey was to Syria, because it is a cold land. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

If it is asked, what is the meaning of God reminding them of the journeys of winter and summer? There are two answers:

One: That in their travels they were safe from the Arabs, because they were the People of the Sanctuary. So He reminded them of this so that they would know His favour upon them in their security, while others feared.

Two: Because they earned, and so they were prosperous, fed others, and gave to the needy (*yasiluna*), as the poet said about them:

*O man who changes his saddle (*rahl*), why did you not stop with the family of 'Abd Manaf?*

*Those who take the covenant from its horizons,*
*and those who set out on the journey of accustomed security (*ilaf*).*

*And those who give the ruined (*al-ra'ishun*)—and there is no one who gives the ruined—*
*and those who say "Come hither" to the guests.*

*And those who mix their rich with their poor,*
*until their poor becomes as one who is sufficient.*

*'Amr al-'Ula crumbled the bread for his people,*
*while the men of Makkah were in drought, emaciated.*

Thus God reminded them of this favour.

[p. 348]

Ibn 'Abbas has a third opinion regarding the journeys of winter and summer: that they would spend winter in Makkah for its warmth, and summer in al-Ta'if for its air, as the poet said:

*Winter in Makkah, a blessing,*
*and its summer in al-Ta'if.*

This is among the great favours, that a people have a hot region that repels the cold of winter from them, and a cold region that repels the heat of summer from them. So God reminded them of this favour.

﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾: God commanded them to worship Him. Regarding His identifying Himself to them as "the Lord of this House," there are two aspects:

One: Because they had idols, so He distinguished Himself from them.

Two: That they were honoured over all the Arabs by the House, so He reminded them of this as a reminder of His favour.

Regarding the meaning of this command, and the *fa'* (so) in His saying ﴿so let them worship﴾, there are four aspects:

First: "So let them worship the Lord of this House," because He bestowed upon them the journeys of winter and summer.

Second: "So let them become accustomed to the worship of the Lord of this House, as they became accustomed to the journeys of winter and summer."

Third: "So let them worship the Lord of this House, because He fed them from hunger and secured them from fear."

Fourth: "So let them abandon the journeys of winter and summer for the worship of the Lord of this House, for He feeds them from hunger and secures them from fear, so that they may devote themselves, by remaining, to supporting His Messenger and defending His religion."

﴿Who fed them from hunger﴾: Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: He fed them from hunger by the wealth He gave them and the provisions He brought to them. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Second: He fed them from hunger by granting the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) concerning them, when he said: ﴿and provide them with fruits﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: That a famine afflicted them in the Jahiliyyah, so God put into the hearts of the Abyssinians to bring them food, and they brought it. The Quraysh feared them and thought they had come to fight them, so they went out to them on guard. But they had brought them food and assisted them with provisions. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿who fed them from hunger﴾.

[p. 349]

﴿And secured them from fear﴾: Regarding this there are four opinions:

First: He secured them from the fear of the Arabs that they might plunder or fight them, out of honour for the sanctity of the Sanctuary, in response to the prior supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: From the fear of the Abyssinians with the Elephant. This was said by al-A'mash.

Third: He secured them from the fear of leprosy (*al-judham*). This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Sufyan al-Thawri.

Fourth: It means He secured the Quraysh so that the caliphate would be only among them. This was said by 'Ali, may God be pleased with him.
